extracted.intended_audience: military officers, Judge Advocate General staff, War Department legal and administrative personnel
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of legal holdings and administrative standards governing duties, appointments, privileges, and procedures affecting Army officers, enlisted men, staff functions, and departmental administration. The page records authoritative "held" rulings and interpretive guidance on specific statutory and regulatory questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain authority before detaching soldier for duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Such authority shall be obtained prior to placing the soldier on duty; this to give the Secretary of War an opportunity to pass on the case before the detachment is made and to make it unnecessary for him to take nunc pro tunc action therein, with a view to avoid imposing hardship upon the soldier, where he is not satisfied that the public interest requires such detachment to be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative detachment of soldiers should be preceded by securing the necessary authority so the Secretary can review and avoid later retroactive action; intended to prevent hardship when Secretary disapproves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 1222 R.S. does not in terms apply to enlisted men
rubrics_metrics.description: On question as to whether an enlisted man could serve as a postmaster, held that the law does not forbid it since section 1222, R. S., does not in terms apply to enlisted men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literal statutory language governs applicability; absence of express mention means the provision is not directly applicable, though other considerations may follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: No legal objection to enlisted man taking post-office oath when acting as mail carrier
rubrics_metrics.description: On question as to whether an enlisted man serving as mail carrier from a post office to a military post might take the 'oath of post-office employees,' held that there was no legal objection to his so doing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oath-taking for certain civil functions by enlisted men is not per se prohibited where statute does not bar it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlisted men generally incompatible with holding civil office despite section 1222 inapplicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1222, R. S., does not apply to enlisted men. But except perhaps in a rare case ... it must in general be quite incompatible with the status and obligation of an enlisted man to hold any civil office or employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where a statute does not explicitly apply, analogy to officer restrictions and the obligations of enlistment usually preclude enlisted men from occupying civil offices; rare exceptions may exist (e.g., certain noncommissioned staff at permanent stations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlisted men should not exercise functions of civil office (Philippine detail example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the statute which provides that an officer who holds civil office by election or appointment vacates his office by such acceptance is not in terms applicable to enlisted men, the analogy prevails and should equally prevent enlisted men from holding or exercising the functions of civil office; Congress intended electrician sergeants to be exclusively employed in Signal Corps and not permanently by Philippine government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive analogy to officer rules and congressional intent can bar enlisted men from foreign civil employment even where statute is silent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties within enlistment contract are permissible details
rubrics_metrics.description: Where enlisted men were detailed to assist an ordnance mechanic in altering the concrete emplacements for guns of the seacoast artillery, held that such duty was that which a soldier is expected to perform under his contract of enlistment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the assigned duty is reasonably within the scope of soldierly duties, the detail is lawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status and protections of a chief musician
rubrics_metrics.description: A chief musician is an enlisted man, but not a noncommissioned officer. He is enlisted not to perform the duties of a soldier, but expressly as an instructor of music. Held that he cannot legally be reduced to the ranks either by sentence or by order; he may be tried by regimental or garrison court as well as by a general court; after the term he may engage in his profession in civil life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special enlistment roles carry particular status and limits on disciplinary reduction; avenues for trial and post-service civil engagement are affirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlisted men served with civil subpoenas outside US exclusive jurisdiction must comply
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an enlisted man who had been served at his post (which was not under the exclusive jurisdiction of the United States) with a subpoena requiring his attendance as a witness before a civil court of the State, neglected to comply, held that he was guilty of contempt, and, if fined by the court, had no remedy; and this though the service was personal and not made through the commanding officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal service of civil process on enlisted personnel stationed outside US exclusive jurisdiction obliges compliance; failure may incur contempt with no remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'Regular Army' vs 'Volunteer Army'
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'Regular Army' simply means the 'Standing Army' — the military organization of the Government, which it is the intention ordinarily to maintain and continue in existence indefinitely ... and this Army is made up of persons who engage voluntarily and directly with the United States to serve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology relates to organizational permanence and method of engagement rather than the manner of raising the force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional designation determines regimental organization and staff entitlement (Porto Rico Regiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although this regiment consists of two battalions, its legal status is that of a regiment of Infantry in the line of the Army, and, as such, it would seem to be entitled to the staff officers pertaining to regiments in the Infantry arm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory designation controls entitlement to staff positions even where unit size or battalion count differs from typical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment language construed as suggestion not restriction (Porto Rico second lieutenants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section ... which provides 'Vacancies ... may be filled by the President ... by the appointment of citizens of Porto Rico whose qualifications ... shall be established by examination,' held not to restrict such appointments to citizens of Porto Rico but to be regarded as a legislative suggestion to the President ... to give especial recognition to the citizens of Porto Rico.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts/administration may construe qualifying statutory phrasing as permissive or advisory rather than mandatory when context indicates suggestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chaplain appointment not statutorily limited by US citizenship (Porto Rico Regiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Held also, that the Porto Rico Regiment of Infantry is entitled to a chaplain, and that as citizenship in the United States is not required by statute as a condition precedent to the appointment of a regimental chaplain, a 'citizen of Porto Rico' can lawfully be appointed chaplain of the Porto Rico Regiment of Infantry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where statute is silent on citizenship requirements for appointment, local citizenship may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philippine Scouts are part of the Regular Army
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that the Philippine Scouts are a part of the Regular Army of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory and administrative classification of units may include colonial/local units as part of Regular Army.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office not a 'bureau' may lie outside statutory prohibition on details
rubrics_metrics.description: On the question of whether, in view of section 4, act of August 5, 1882, a master gunner could be detailed for duty in the office of the Chief of Artillery, held that that office was not a bureau of the War Department and did not therefore come within the inhibition of the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterization of an office (bureau vs non-bureau) affects applicability of statutes restricting details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captains and lieutenants not required for company duty may be placed on 'unassigned list' for staff duty
rubrics_metrics.description: The quoted portion of said section 6 is to be construed as ... referring ... to officers of those grades 'not required for duty with batteries or companies.' ... authorizing the War Department to adopt the necessary and appropriate means for carrying the provision into effect; that therefore if the Secretary of War is convinced that the end contemplated can be best accomplished by carrying captains and lieutenants needed for such staff duty and other details upon an 'unassigned list' such means are, under the language quoted, legislatively sanctioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative recognition permits administrative placement of surplus officers on unassigned lists to be used for staff and other authorized details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Towing subcaliber practice targets over lobster-pot areas does not automatically create gov't liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that targets for subcaliber practice can be towed over areas within which are 'lobster pots' without subjecting the Government to a claim for damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational activities over third-party property do not always give rise to liability; context and risk allocation matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Army staff officers are under immediate direction of Secretary of War
rubrics_metrics.description: The staff of the Army, consisting of the General Staff and the chiefs of the Staff Corps and inferior officers of the same, constitute the staff of the Commander in Chief of the Army — the President. As such, these officers are properly under the immediate direction of the Secretary of War, who acts for the President in the administration of the military department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chain of administrative direction places staff functions under the Secretary for departmental administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Staff officers detailed to staff cannot succeed to territorial department command
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of the President detailing an officer for duty in the General Staff places in temporary abeyance the office held by such officer in the arm of service ... and during the period of his incumbency of office in the General Staff he becomes as fully an officer of the staff as if he held a permanent appointment therein. During such incumbency he is as powerless to exercise command in the line ... as would be the case if he were a permanent officer of the Staff Corps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary detail to General Staff suspends line-office command authority; succession rules follow incumbency status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjutant General as central record-keeping channel
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be some office in which the action of the Secretary of War, in respect to the duty to which officers of the Army are assigned, shall be made a matter of official record; ... The Adjutant General ... constitutes the channel of communication between the heads of departments and the Secretary of War in such cases ... and in his office the record of the action of the Secretary thereon is made a matter of permanent record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralized records (stations, duties, efficiency reports) are essential for administration, pay, retirement, and can be called for by the Secretary or required by statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspector General special inspection reports are confidential
rubrics_metrics.description: Held that the reports of special inspections by the Inspector General's Department are confidential documents and that the testimony taken is taken as a part and parcel of such reports. There is no law or regulation which requires copies of the evidence contained in these confidential reports to be furnished to officers whose conduct has been under investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidentiality of inspection reports limits disclosure to investigated officers absent specific law/regulation authorizing disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of the Judge Advocate General (enumerated functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The work done in the office of the Judge Advocate General ... consists mainly of the following particulars: Reviewing and making reports upon proceedings of trials by court-martial ... making reports upon applications for pardon or mitigation of sentence; preparing and revising charges and specifications prior to trial ... drafting of contracts, bonds, deeds, leases, licenses, grants of rights of way, approvals of location of rights of way, approvals of plans ... framing of bills, forms of procedure, preparing opinions upon questions relating to the appointment, promotion, rank, pay, allowances ... the civil rights, liabilities and relations of military persons ... interpretation and effect of public contracts ... validity and disposition of claims against the United States ... execution of public works under appropriations by Congress; upon obstructions to navigation ... riparian rights ... and furnishing statements and information apposite to claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JAG office performs broad legal advisory, drafting, prosecutorial, and claims-related functions for the War Department; duties include confidential opinions and varied legal instruments for execution by the Secretary of War.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge Advocate General reports are confidential communications
rubrics_metrics.description: The reports of the Judge Advocate General to the Secretary of War have always been regarded as confidential communications and it has not been the practice to furnish copies of them to parties outside the department in the absence of special authority from the Secretary of War.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JAG reports are ordinarily withheld from external parties unless Secretary authorizes disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge Advocate General lacks administrative jurisdiction over reporters' claims for court-martial proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Judge Advocate General has no administrative jurisdiction over claims of parties employed to report the proceedings of court-martials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims arising from contracted reporters fall outside JAG's administrative remit and must be pursued through appropriate channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge Advocate General generally will not issue opinions on internal State affairs or military administration of a State upon external request
rubrics_metrics.description: It is contrary to the practice of the Judge Advocate General's Office to give, upon request of the military officers or the officials of a State, opinions on questions arising in the military administration of the State. Similarly held with respect to requests made directly to the Judge Advocate General for opinions upon questions relating to any other internal affairs of a State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JAG exercises prudence in confining advisory opinions to federal military matters; requests regarding State internal affairs are typically declined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detail to bonded supply department does not exempt officer from bond requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A line officer serving by detail under the act of February 2, 1901, in a supply department, the officers of which are required to be bonded, is not exempt from a bond simply because his office in such department vested in the operation of a detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory bond requirements attach to functions/positions, not to the method (detail vs permanent) by which the officer occupies them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate appropriation funds street-car tickets depending on message nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost of street-car tickets necessary in the delivery of commercial messages from Alaska telegraph and cable lines should be paid, in the case of commercial messages, out of the appropriation for the operation of lines; if for purely military messages, tickets should be furnished by the Quartermaster's Department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charge expenses to the appropriation serving the nature (commercial vs military) of the message delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractors transporting troops through foreign territory should obtain consent or provide alternate routing
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract was made for the transportation in time of peace of troops and supplies over a route, a part of which was in foreign territory, held that the contractor should obtain written consent of the foreign government to the passage of troops, and in the event of its being impossible to obtain such consent suggested that a stipulation be inserted requiring the contractor in such a case to carry the troops by another route without additional cost to the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procurement contracts for foreign transit should include clauses securing foreign consent and alternatives to protect US interests and avoid extra cost; also include protection against customs charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transportation of Government supplies through foreign territory generally treated as ordinary commerce in peacetime
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule of international law applicable to troops, that a State must obtain express permission before its troops can pass through the territory of another State, does not apply in time of peace to the transportation of Government supplies through foreign territory in the ordinary course of foreign commerce, and duties are not, as a rule, levied on such goods while in course of transportation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial shipment of supplies abroad is generally permissible without the troop-passage consent requirement, but shipments approaching troop movement (guns, horses with soldiers in uniform) should be treated cautiously and consent sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entitlement to transportation on discharge without honor from territorial possessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier is discharged without honor in Alaska, or other territorial possession of the United States, and is not entitled to travel allowances, held that he is not entitled to transportation in kind at the cost of the United States, but may be conveyed to the United States on a Government or chartered transport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discharge status and statutory travel-allowance entitlements determine whether transportation-in-kind is payable; alternative conveyance may nonetheless be provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pensionable status for contracted transport seamen if killed or wounded performing duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that under the act of May 28, 1896, masters, mates, pilots, and engineers on vessels that are being used as transports by contract, if killed or wounded while performing such duties, have the same pensionable status as soldiers and sailors serving in the Army and Navy of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracted vessel personnel performing transport duties may acquire pensionable status equivalent to uniformed personnel when injured/killed in service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers served with summons in seaman's wage suits should respond and notify authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: When a contract exists ... recommended that officers summoned in suits instituted in the United States courts for seaman's wages should respond; the officer whose duty it becomes to make response should forthwith notify the proper United States district attorney of the institution of the suit and request him to defend the same, and at the same time report action to the War Department ... so that the Attorney General may be requested to give the district attorney any required instructions in the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural duties on being served include prompt response, notification of district attorney, and reporting to War Department to coordinate defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition of found money on transport by officers
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer took possession of found money ($15.65) as the finder, which was valid against all the world except the true owner. He could retain the money subject to claim by the true owner or he could turn it over to the transport quartermaster. The latter, upon the receipt of such money, should take it up as 'found on U. S. Army transport,' and turn it into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finders' rights limited by true-owner claims; turning found money into official quartermaster channels for Treasury receipt is proper practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act of April 28, 1904 American-vessel requirement applies to Philippine Islands
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of April 28, 1904 ... which provides for the transportation 'by sea' of supplies for the Army and Navy in American vessels applies to the transportation of military supplies by sea in the Philippine Islands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes requiring use of American vessels for government shipments extend to insular possessions unless otherwise specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility for transportation of families/employees depends on acquired status
rubrics_metrics.description: Held under the act of June 12, 1906 ... that a person who has not yet acquired the above status is not entitled to transportation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory conditions precedent (status acquisition) determine entitlement to transportation benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraterritoriality principle limited for public vessels
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of exterritoriality is one which is applied to vessels of war in the territorial waters of a foreign power. It is by no means well established that public vessels as distinguished from public armed vessels are entitled to the privilege, and the rule itself does not control in the relations between a consul general of the United States (or a consul) in a foreign port and the master of an Army transport in the employ of the Quartermaster General.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume full extraterritorial privileges apply to all public vessels; evaluate vessel character and diplomatic relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 1765 R.S. does not apply to increased money allowance on transports due to local high costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Held that section 1765 R. S., forbidding any officer in the public service ... to receive any additional pay ... unless the same is authorized by law, has no application to an increase in the money allowance on a transport due to the excessive cost of beef in Alaska, and does not require the cost of subsistence of passengers on a transport to be raised, due to the high cost of supplies in Alaska.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowances tied to operational necessities and local cost adjustments may not be treated as unauthorized 'additional pay' under section 1765; context and statutory interpretation matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quartermaster Department may issue transportation requests good on automobile lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Held that when an officer in the Philippine Islands is ordered to travel in the military service, and the only transportation along a portion of the journey is by automobile, a transportation request may be furnished by the Quartermaster's Department, good on the automobile line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transportation instruments may be adapted to available modes (e.g., automobiles) when serving a governmental travel order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quartermaster purchase from officer requires Secretary of War approval
rubrics_metrics.description: On a question as to whether a quartermaster could buy a horse for the Government from an officer of the Army, held that unless such purchase received the approval of the Secretary of War it would not be valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transactions with officers creating potential conflict or self-dealing need high-level approval to be valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of stores to retired officers allowed by executive regulation in some cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale of stores to officers on the retired list is now authorized by Executive regulation in some cases — notably that of subsistence stores. As such stores ... are sold at the cost price, and as such sales are authorized to be made to 'officers of the Army' and are not restricted, by statute, to officers on the active list, there is no legal objection to the sale of forage to retired officers at cost price, under such restrictions ... as may be imposed by the Secretary of War.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive regulations can authorize certain sales to retired officers; Secretary may impose quantity/condition restrictions; legislative sanction unnecessary where analogously authorized for subsistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mess liability for commissary charges apportioned among members
rubrics_metrics.description: Held that such mess was not in the nature of a commercial partnership ... but was simply an association ... each of whom was bound to the United States only for his proportion — one-third — of the account. And held that a member who had paid his proportion to one of the other members who acted as caterer but who had deceased without paying over this amount to the commissary, remained liable for such proportion to the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members of informal messes are individually liable for their shares; payments to a fellow member do not discharge liability to the United States unless paid to the government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue of stores beyond established rations is unlawful
rubrics_metrics.description: The issue of stores for food beyond amounts fixed in established rations, held not lawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationing rules are strict; deviations that exceed statutory or regulatory allowance lack lawful authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual rations can constitute lawful waiver of regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where employees of the Alaskan telegraph lines, receiving over $60 per month, were issued rations because no other method of subsistence was practicable, such issue being incorporated in their contracts of employment, held to be a waiver of the requirements of par. 1219, Army Regulations, 1904 ed., which it was lawful for the Secretary of War to make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contract terms incorporated into employment and approved by Secretary may validly alter standard regulatory requirements when necessity exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issuance of rations in kind where subsistence unobtainable
rubrics_metrics.description: Where other subsistence cannot be obtained at places in Alaska, held that female nurses, and enlisted patients in hospital may be issued rations in kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical necessity in remote locations permits in-kind ration issuance for personnel otherwise unable to obtain subsistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief of Ordnance lacks statutory authorization under section 1167 to prescribe inspection-for-condemnation system
rubrics_metrics.description: Held that section 1167, R. S., does not direct or authorize the Chief of Ordnance, subject to the approval of the Secretary of War, to draw up and enforce in his department a system of rules and regulations for the inspection of ordnance property with a view to its condemnation and sale or destruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority to establish condemnation/sale systems for ordnance property requires clear statutory delegation; section 1167 insufficient for such rulemaking authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line officers detailed in Ordnance Dept must take promotion examinations in line; equivalency may excuse certain branches
rubrics_metrics.description: A line officer, detailed for service in the Ordnance Department ... is required to take the examination for promotion in the line which is provided for in section 3 of the act of October 1, 1890. In the application the principle of equivalency ... held that he may lawfully be excused from examination in those branches in which he has passed a successful examination for detail in the Ordnance Department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotion-exam obligations follow statutory promotion scheme; prior successful ordnance detail examinations can provide equivalency relief for certain branch exams under General Order guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification for second detail in Ordnance Dept is recommendation-based, not an 'examination'
rubrics_metrics.description: The verification of capacity and fitness for a second detail in the Ordnance Department is, in the act of June 25, 1906, made to depend upon the recommendation of a board of ordnance officers, but ... it is not an 'examination' in the sense in which that term is used in the acts regulating the advancement of officers ... General Order 220 ... is not such as to exempt an ordnance officer from the operation of existing orders regulating the examination for promotion of officers in his branch of the line of the Army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different statutory or order-based processes (board recommendation vs statutory examination) have distinct legal consequences; the label 'examination' matters for applicability of promotion rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 1765 does not prohibit compensation to ordnance sergeant for non-affined work
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that section 1765, R. S., does not prohibit the payment of compensation to an ordnance sergeant for work as 'time keeper' under the United States Engineer Department, such employment having no affinity or connection with the line of his official duty as ordnance sergeant and not interfering in any way with the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payments for distinct, non-conflicting extra duties may be permissible even where section 1765 restricts unauthorized additional compensation; evaluate affinity and interference with official duty.
